channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] North Carolina Ports hit by intrusion that took cargo processing systems offline across three facilities
item.description: The North Carolina State Ports Authority detected an unauthorised intrusion on 4 August that triggered a systems-wide IT outage across all three of its maritime logistics hubs: the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port. Processing workflows were directly affected, with truck movements, cargo processing and administrative systems disrupted while restoration was underway. Terminal operations and vessel activity continued as scheduled, and some cargo processing shifted to manual handling. The incident is a clean illustration of a pattern this sector keeps repeating: the ships kept moving and the cranes kept working, but the paperwork layer that tells the terminal what to move and releases it to a trucker went down, and that is enough to back up a gate queue and ripple into inland rail-served facilities. - North Carolina State Ports Authority — reported by Splash247 and Cybernews - Detected 4 Aug 2026; reporting through Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Treasury names an Iranian intelligence-directed hacking network operating inside US critical infrastructure
item.description: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security–directed hacking group on 24 August, within a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels. Five alleged operators, described as tied to the Mabna Institute, were indicted by the Justice Department the preceding week. Treasury says the network has been breaching and exfiltrating data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. The scope is worth reading precisely: what is attributed here is espionage and data theft, not manipulation of process equipment. The State Department has posted a $10 million reward on related activity. For marine and port operators the designation carries two distinct consequences. The first is intrusion risk: the victim set Treasury names — energy companies, defence contractors, IT firms — overlaps heavily with the charterers, bunker suppliers, shipyards and managed service providers that sit in a terminal’s or a fleet’s supply chain, and access collected for espionage converts to disruption when tasking changes. The second is compliance, and it is more immediate. The wider action covers vessels as well as people and companies, spanning Iranian oil, shipping and digital-asset networks. Any operator involved in chartering, port agency, bunkering or cargo handling should assume its sanctions screening lists changed on 24 August, and that a vessel or counterparty cleared last week may not clear this week. - US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; Department of Justice indictment; State Department Rewards for Justice notice — via The Hacker News, CyberScoop and Nextgov/FCW - Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; DOJ indictments the preceding week; trade-press analysis 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CEVA Logistics breach affects European warehouses and spills customer data through its retail clients
item.description: CEVA Logistics, one of the world’s largest shipping and logistics operators, was attacked between 29 July and 1 August, with the intrusion affecting at least eight warehouses across Europe. The France-headquartered company runs more than a thousand warehouses worldwide and reported 18.3 billion dollars in revenue last year. The consequences surfaced indirectly: several companies that rely on CEVA for fulfilment disclosed that their customers’ personal information was taken in the breach, including Dutch e-commerce group Bol, department store De Bijenkorf, eyewear company Ace & Tate, football club Ajax, and Steam’s European hardware business. For marine and port operators the lesson is about position in the chain rather than the specific victim: a third-party logistics provider holds consignee data, routing detail and warehouse operations for hundreds of shippers at once, so one compromise produces notification obligations across a long list of unrelated customers. - TechCrunch, corroborated by The Record and The Register - Attack 29 Jul–1 Aug 2026; reported 10–11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Five federal agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers, commercial facilities in scope
item.description: The NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August warning that threat actors are combining the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 libraries with AI-assisted scripting to build tools that mimic legitimate OT monitoring software, giving read and write access to Siemens S7 controller memory, configuration data and ladder logic over S7comm. Critical manufacturing, energy, water, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities are named as the most-targeted sectors. Actors locate exposed devices using internet scanning services and gain access through default or weakly configured credentials rather than a vulnerability. Affected lines span the S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 including F-series safety controllers. Shoreside terminals are squarely inside the commercial facilities scope: S7 and comparable controllers run bulk and conveyor handling, shore power, fuelling systems, gate barriers and terminal building services, and many were commissioned by an integrator with remote access still enabled. - Joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Issued 19 Aug 2026; reported 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
item.description: CISA published AA26-237A on 25 August comparing two red-team assessments run with near-identical tradecraft: one against a government services and facilities organisation, one against a water and wastewater systems entity. Both opened with phishing and escalated through Active Directory weaknesses that are ordinary rather than exotic — a Machine Account Quota left at its default of 10, and misconfigured Active Directory Certificate Services templates. The outcomes diverged sharply. At the organisation CISA labels A, the team obtained elevated domain privileges and reached sensitive business systems and cloud resources without ever being detected, despite the organisation running multiple security operations centres and multiple EDR products. CISA’s stated reason deserves reading twice: the SOCs did not communicate with one another, and thousands of false positives from routine business activity buried the real signal. Port authorities, terminal operators and ship managers should read this as a description of their own environment. The corporate Active Directory that this tradecraft targets is very often the same directory authenticating terminal operating system clients, gate and crane HMI workstations, and the shoreside servers that hold vessel performance and cargo data. Both weaknesses named are free to fix. The detection finding is the harder one for this sector: monitoring is frequently split between a corporate IT team, a port-wide MSSP and an OT integrator, which is precisely the multi-console arrangement in which CISA found alerts going uncorrelated. - CISA cybersecurity advisory AA26-237A — joint red-team assessment findings - Published 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Baltic GNSS spoofing is a coordinated transmitter network, not scattered jamming — and its footprint now reaches seven states
item.description: Two independent lines of evidence hardened a picture the maritime industry has been treating as background noise. Lithuania’s communications regulator reported on 18 August that spoofing antennae operating from Kaliningrad have grown from three in early 2025 to 36, giving a broadcast radius of roughly 450 km that now covers Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Finland, Sweden, Belarus and the Baltic itself. Separately, researchers from GPSPatron and Gdynia Maritime University published shore-based and at-sea measurements taken aboard the research vessel Imor near the Polish coast and the Kaliningrad maritime boundary. They identified four distinct transmitter types at four locations that switched on and off together — the signature of centralised tactical control rather than opportunistic interference. Every recorded event combined multi-constellation jamming with false GPS L1 signals, meaning receivers were not merely denied a fix but handed a plausible wrong one. That distinction matters on a bridge: a jammed receiver alarms, a spoofed one does not. The researchers describe effects on ECDIS, on some autopilot implementations, and on the position picture VTS operators use to sequence traffic. For operators this is electronic warfare rather than a network compromise, but the operational consequence — a watch team, a pilot and a port that cannot agree where a vessel is — belongs in the same resilience planning as a cyber incident, and it is now a standing condition in a major European trade lane rather than an occasional event. - GPSPatron / Gdynia Maritime University field study reported by The Maritime Executive; Lithuanian regulator figures reported 18 Aug 2026 - Regulator reporting 18 Aug 2026; field study published Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Six agencies warn the Gunra ransomware crew is walking into critical infrastructure through two 2025 Fortinet bugs
item.description: CISA, the FBI, the Defense Cyber Crime Center, the NSA, the Secret Service and the Korean National Police Agency published joint advisory AA26-222A on 10 August on Gunra, a ransomware operation that has hit organisations across critical infrastructure sectors since April 2025. The advisory’s operational point is unglamorous: Gunra’s initial access is overwhelmingly through internet-facing edge devices, and specifically two Fortinet flaws — CVE-2024-21762 and CVE-2024-55591 — both patched in 2025 and both still reachable on unpatched appliances. Once inside, the group steals data before encrypting, and runs a double-extortion leak site. The agencies published detection guidance, indicators and a set of mitigations centred on patching edge appliances, enforcing phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication and segmenting recovery infrastructure. Ports, terminals and maritime logistics firms sit in the critical-infrastructure set this advisory covers, and the route in is the perimeter appliance rather than anything maritime-specific. North Carolina Ports has just shown what an IT-side outage does to gate throughput; Gunra’s pattern — steal, then encrypt — produces the same manual-operations outcome with a data-leak tail attached. - CISA / FBI / DC3 / NSA / USSS / ROK National Police joint advisory AA26-222A — reported by The Record and Infosecurity Magazine - Published 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] Industrial ransomware rose 12 percent in Q2, and disrupted output without touching control systems
item.description: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up from 1,020 in the first quarter, with manufacturing accounting for 747, construction 176, equipment manufacturing 114 and food and beverage 70. The finding most relevant to ports and vessel operators concerns mechanism rather than sector counts: disrupting the IT systems supporting an industrial environment is regularly sufficient to interrupt operations even when attackers never reach the control system, and extortion continued shifting from file encryption toward data theft. The North Carolina Ports outage is a textbook instance — cranes and berths unaffected, cargo processing halted. For vessel operators the equivalent exposure sits in fleet management, planned maintenance, crewing and charter systems ashore, whose loss disrupts commercial operation long before anything on the bridge is at risk. - Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis — via Help Net Security - Published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA sets a three-day federal deadline on a CVSS 10.0 Oracle web-tier flaw now under active attack
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-21962 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 24 August with a remediation date of 27 August — the tightest window Binding Operational Directive 26-04 permits. The flaw is an improper access control issue in Oracle HTTP Server and in the Oracle WebLogic Server Proxy Plug-in for Apache HTTP Server and Microsoft IIS, scored CVSS 10.0. It is reachable over HTTP by an unauthenticated attacker with no user interaction and no existing privileges, and successful exploitation allows access to the instance or modification of the data it fronts. Oracle shipped the fix in its January 2026 critical patch update; reporting on 25 August describes broad exploitation against WebLogic servers. A three-day federal deadline is the signal worth reading — CISA reserves that window for exploitation it judges both live and consequential. This is not an ICS product and it will not be on a vessel, but Oracle’s web tier is a very common reverse proxy in front of the shoreside applications a port runs: terminal operating system web clients, port community systems, appointment and gate booking portals, EDI and customs interfaces, and the reporting layers that expose berth and yard data to carriers and truckers. Those are the systems whose loss produces exactly the manual-processing scenario North Carolina Ports worked through earlier this month. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition; Oracle critical patch update — corroborated by SecurityWeek and The Hacker News - Added to KEV 24 Aug 2026; federal remediation deadline 27 Aug 2026; Oracle fix issued Jan 2026; broad exploitation reported 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Citrix is telling admins to patch NetScaler now — an unauthenticated bypass on the appliance that fronts most OT remote access
item.description: Citrix published bulletin CTX696939 on 20 August covering two NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway flaws. The serious one, CVE-2026-19490, is an authentication bypass carrying a CVSS score of 9.3: on Gateway and AAA virtual-server configurations an unauthenticated attacker can skip the login step entirely. The second, CVE-2026-19489, is a memory overflow that can produce unpredictable behaviour or a denial of service, and only applies where SIP ALG is enabled on a Large Scale NAT group. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.32 and 13.1-63.21 or later. Citrix, Rapid7 and Finland’s national cyber authority all said they were not aware of in-the-wild exploitation at publication, while urging immediate patching — NetScaler has a long record of exploited edge flaws. In the maritime sector NetScaler tends to sit in front of terminal operating system access for shipping lines, customs brokers and haulage partners, and increasingly in front of shoreside access to vessel management platforms. An authentication bypass on that appliance reaches straight into the systems that decide whether a gate opens and a box moves. - Citrix security bulletin CTX696939 — reported by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News - Bulletin published 20 Aug 2026; reported 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Fire-alarm management software stores its credentials in cleartext in memory, CISA warns
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-232-01 on 20 August covering Johnson Controls Simplex Incident Manager, the software operators use to monitor and manage Simplex fire alarm panels across a property portfolio. Versions up to and including V2.01 keep user passwords and authentication tokens unencrypted in system memory while the application runs, tracked as CVE-2026-27875 and classified as CWE-316. A local attacker who already holds low-privileged access to the workstation can read those credentials out of memory and reuse them against the application and the systems it connects to. CISA lists critical manufacturing, commercial facilities, government facilities, transportation systems and energy among the affected sectors, with deployment worldwide. Johnson Controls has published remediation guidance in JCI-PSA-2026-28. Terminals, cruise facilities and port administration buildings run Simplex fire detection, and on a port estate the fire-alarm management workstation is often shared, physically accessible and administered by a facilities contractor. That is the local low-privileged foothold this flaw needs, and the credentials it yields reach every panel on the property. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-232-01; Johnson Controls product security advisory JCI-PSA-2026-28 - Published 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco ASA and FTD VPN zero-day exploited to reload firewalls, added to CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco has patched CVE-2026-20349, a flaw in the remote-access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure Firewall Threat Defense software that attackers are exploiting to force appliances offline. A specially crafted HTTP request to the vulnerable service causes an unexpected reload and a denial-of-service condition, requiring no authentication and no user interaction. Cisco’s PSIRT confirmed active exploitation in August, and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Hot fixes cover ASA 9.16, 9.18, 9.20, 9.22, 9.23 and 9.24 and FTD 7.0, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6, 7.7 and 10.0. In a maritime context these appliances typically terminate the links carrying vendor support into terminal systems, shore-to-ship connectivity, and remote access for staff at inland and satellite facilities — so an attacker can remove your remote support path at the moment you most need it. - Cisco security advisory and CISA KEV catalogue — reported by Help Net Security and SecurityWeek - Exploitation confirmed and KEV listed Aug 2026; reported 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] August ICS Patch Tuesday: maximum-severity missing authentication in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced
item.description: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The most severe, SSA-834709, is a maximum-severity missing authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with elevated privileges. Siemens also fixed a critical code execution vulnerability in Siveillance Video Management Servers and high-severity flaws in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and Logo! Soft Comfort, with medium-severity issues in Ruggedcom devices and Desigo controllers. Schneider Electric published advisories for NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, and Phoenix Contact one covering multiple PLCnext firmware flaws. Two of these land squarely in port estates: Siveillance is a video management platform widely deployed for terminal and perimeter surveillance under facility security plans, and Ruggedcom switches are common in harsh-environment terminal and quayside networks. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact advisories — summarised by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Four more exploited flaws added to KEV on 18 August, including Windows IKE and VMware vCenter
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August: CVE-2026-33824 in Microsoft Internet Key Exchange, CVE-2026-55040 in Microsoft SharePoint, CVE-2026-59310 in Broadcom VMware vCenter and CVE-2026-65400 in Apple macOS. Two further additions followed on 20 August, both in TrueConf Server. For port and vessel operators the IKE and vCenter entries carry the most weight. IKE terminates the site-to-site tunnels linking terminals, inland facilities and headquarters, and frequently the shore end of vessel connectivity. vCenter typically manages the virtual infrastructure hosting terminal operating systems, berth planning and historians — a compromise there is a hypervisor-level problem affecting everything running on it. SharePoint is worth a second look in this sector specifically because facility and vessel security plan documentation, procedures and drawings are so often stored there. - CISA KEV catalogue additions - Added 18 Aug 2026; two further additions 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA publishes an advisory for flaws in Malcolm, its own free OT monitoring suite
item.description: Advisory ICSA-26-230-01 covers vulnerabilities in Malcolm, the network traffic analysis suite CISA distributes free for OT and ICS environments, which could let an attacker cause a denial-of-service condition or execute arbitrary code. Affected versions are below 26.06.1, below 26.07.0 and up to and including 26.07.1. On the same day CISA published ICSA-26-230-02, a stack overflow in Siemens Simcenter Nastran that can lead to remote code execution if a user is tricked into running the affected binary with a malicious string; Siemens has released fixed versions. Malcolm turns up more often in this sector than expected, because smaller port authorities and terminal operators without a commercial OT monitoring budget deploy it to satisfy visibility expectations under the Coast Guard rule — typically on a span or tap seeing the whole terminal network, and typically outside the patch inventory. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-230-01 and ICSA-26-230-02 - Published 18 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] A low-privilege Metasys user can plant a payload that runs in an administrator’s browser
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-14, published 13 August, describes a stored cross-site scripting flaw in Johnson Controls Metasys. A user with low privileges can inject a payload through a crafted URL; the payload persists across logins and then executes in the browser context of anyone who subsequently views it, administrators included. Metasys 12, 13, 14 and 15 are affected. That is a privilege-escalation path inside the building management platform rather than a remote takeover, and there is no report of exploitation. Metasys turns up across port authority administrative buildings, terminal offices, cold-storage sheds and cruise terminals, usually managed by a facilities contractor rather than the OT team. The flaw itself is modest, but it grants a foothold that executes with administrator context inside the platform that runs terminal HVAC and, at many facilities, feeds door control — and BMS estates are habitually excluded from the port’s vulnerability management scope entirely. - CISA ICSA-26-225-14 — Johnson Controls product security advisory - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Coast Guard cyber rule: annual training already required, Cybersecurity Plans due 16 July 2027
item.description: The Coast Guard’s Cybersecurity in the Marine Transportation System rule, codified at 33 CFR Part 101 Subpart F, took effect on 16 July 2025 and applies to owners and operators of US-flagged vessels, Outer Continental Shelf facilities and facilities regulated under the Maritime Transportation Security Act. Two dates govern current planning. Personnel training required under 33 CFR 101.650 has been mandatory since 12 January 2026 and recurs annually. The substantive deadline is 16 July 2027, by which point owners and operators must have designated a Cybersecurity Officer, conducted a Cybersecurity Assessment, and submitted a Cybersecurity Plan to the Coast Guard for review and approval. The Coast Guard has also signalled increased Port State Control attention to poor cybersecurity practice, where findings can produce deficiencies, detention, denial of entry or Captain of the Port restrictions on vessel movement. - US Coast Guard final rule, Federal Register — codified at 33 CFR Part 101 Subpart F - Rule effective 16 Jul 2025; training since 12 Jan 2026; plans due 16 Jul 2027

item.title: [Low] US and Australian agencies publish guidance on isolating OT and operating that way for an extended period
item.description: A joint publication from US and Australian agencies sets out how critical infrastructure operators should prepare to isolate vital operational technology and supporting systems from external connectivity, and to keep operating in that isolated state for an extended period rather than the few hours most continuity plans assume. It is guidance, not a requirement. Its value in a maritime context is that it converts a claim most terminals make confidently — that they can work cargo on paper if systems go down — into a dependency checklist covering time synchronisation, authentication, licence servers, customs and cargo release interfaces, and the physical availability of staff who have done it before. The North Carolina Ports incident is a live example of the scenario: terminal operations continued while processing shifted to manual, and the constraint was documentation flow rather than machinery. - Joint US–Australian OT isolation guidance — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 29 Jul 2026
